0Differentiable Manifolds

2.

Prove that the tangent bundle of a differentiable manifold is orientable (even though M may not be).

Let π be the projection from TM to M. Cover M with {(U,φ)}, then {π−1(U)} covers TM=π−1(M), and we need to find the trivialization φ~​ associated to π−1(U) for each U.

Given any smooth chart φ:U⊂M→Rn, define φ~​:π−1(U)⊂TM→R2n by v∣p​↦(φ(p),v).For any two overlapping charts (U,φ) and (V,ψ), the transition map ψ~​∘φ~​−1:φ(U∩V)×Rn→ψ(U∩V)×Rn is given by (x,v)↦(x~,∂x∂x~​v),where ψ∘φ−1(x):=x~(x)=(x~1(x),⋯,x~n(x)). Then the determinant is (det∂x∂x~​)2>0.

Exercise 2 provides a local isometry π:Rn→Tn, but there is no local isometry ρ:Tn→Rn. Indeed, write ρ=(ρ1​,⋯,ρn​). ρ1​ mapping the compact set Tn to R attains its maximum at some p∈Tn, and consequently dρ1​(p)=0∈Rn. Then dρ(p)=(0,⋯)∈Rn×n is singular.

7.

Method I. Consider the cone C tangent to S2 along c, then the parallel transport of V0​ along c is the same, whether taken relative to S2 or to C, as the tangent spaces along c whether taken relative to S2 or to C are the same. Flatten the cone (locally, or at least minus a line) to a sector on the plane (in other words, C is locally isometric to a sector in R2 with c being its arc). The parallel transport of V0​ on the plane is merely translation in R2. From the perspective of a person walking along c, V0​ appears to be rotating at constant speed, reminiscent of a scene when the theme song of Detective Conan goes ‘運命のルーレット廻して、ずっと君を見ていた’. For details, refer to [dC] 4-4 Example 1 (p.246).

Method II. Consider the cone C tangent to S2 along c, parametrized as {(avcosu,avsinu,bv)∈R3:u,v∈R},where a2+b2=1. The parallel transport of V0​ along c is the same, whether taken relative to S2 or to C, as the tangent spaces along c whether taken relative to S2 or to C are the same. Now we carry out a bit of calculations to see the effect of parallel–translating V0​ along c, written U(t)∂u​+V(t)∂v​. Besides, let u(t)=t,v(t)=v0​ be the local expression for c(t). First, guu​=a2v2,guv​=0,gvv​=1,and then Γuuu​=0,Γvuu​=v1​,Γuuv​=−a2v,Γvuv​=0.Substituting into {U˙+(Γuuu​u˙+Γuvu​v˙)U+(Γvuu​u˙+Γvvu​v˙)V=0,V˙+(Γuuv​u˙+Γuvv​v˙)U+(Γvuv​u˙+Γvvv​v˙)V=0,​where u˙=1,v˙=0, we get ⎩⎨⎧​U˙+ v1​ V=0,V˙−a2vU=0.​Hence, {​U= c cos(at+d),V=av0​sin(at+d)​for two constants c,d. We conclude that the vector rotates at angular velocity a, if the angular velocity of c along the parallel is taken to be 1.

Let {pn​} be a Cauchy sequence in M, that is, d(pn​,pm​)→0. Then d(f(pn​),f(pm​))→0 too. As M is complete, {f(pn​)} converges to some point in M, written f(p), for f is surjective. Then {pn​} converges to p, as f is a diffeomorphism.

Were f not injective, i.e. f(p)=f(q) for two distinct points p,q∈M, then for a geodesic γ joining p to q, f∘γ is a loop. Because f is a local isometry, f∘γ is a geodesic too. Take any point r different from f(p) in the image of f∘γ, then there are two geodesics joining f(p) to r, a contradiction.

Next we show that f is surjective. For any s∈M, let γˉ​ be the geodesic segment joining f(p) to s, where f(p) is any point in the image of f. Let γ be the geodesic starting from p with initial speed v such that dfp​(v)=γˉ​′(0). Then γˉ​ is precisely f∘γ as both are geodesics that start from f(p) with the same initial speed, and it follows that (f∘γ)(l(γˉ​))=s, where owing to the completeness of M, γ is defined on the entire [0,∞), and in particular at l(γˉ​).

Here we used the fact that a local isometry M→f(M) maps geodesics γ to geodesics f∘γ (mentioned on p.73). The reason: The geodesic equation depends on the metric and its first derivatives in a coordinate chart. A local isometry preserves the metric and is a local diffeomorphism. So it induces coordinates on f(M) with the same metric coefficients. In particular, it must take geodesics to geodesics.

If K≥0 instead, M=R×Sn−1 violates the theorem.

Remark: Cf. [YS] 1.2 (pp.13–7) for the proof of the splitting theorem (Cheeger–Gromoll, 1971) below.

Let M be an n-dimensional complete Riemannian manifold with Ric(M)≥0. Suppose that M has a line. Then M is isometric to R×N, where N is an (n−1)-dimensional Riemannian manifold with the product metric.
